# Jeuxvideo.com — French contemporary review

- Original source: [Jeuxvideo.com — French contemporary review](https://www.jeuxvideo.com/articles/0000/00002646_test.htm)
- Author / publication: pilou / Jeuxvideo.com
- Language / date: French; 2002-11-22
- Access: Full review page retrieved directly
- Checked: 2026-09-09
- Retrieved: 2026-09-09
- Archived copy: [Wayback Machine, 2025-01-19](http://web.archive.org/web/20250119154348/https://www.jeuxvideo.com/articles/0000/00002646_test.htm)
- Format: header notes, original summary, then complete factual notes (commercial review, not transcribed)

The reviewer argues that direct fighting can overwhelm the intended stealth-and-tactics design. Guards are described as forgiving enough that force can bypass more elaborate abilities, while controlling several fighters can become disorderly.

Detailed 2D environments receive praise, although visual density and the fixed viewpoint can obscure interactive objects. The review finds some innovations appealing but questions how well combat and infiltration fit together. Repetitive voices are another criticism.

Visible category scores are graphics 15/20, playability 12/20, longevity 14/20, sound 13/20, and scenario 12/20. The overall numeric editorial score was not exposed in the inspected article text, so it is not inferred from those categories.

**Research use:** a contemporary critique of stealth incentives, encounter balance, and scene readability.

## Detailed notes

Page facts: published 22/11/2002 at 18:00; author "pilou", journalist at jeuxvideo.com; category scores graphics 15/20, playability 12/20, lifespan 14/20, sound 13/20, scenario 12/20; 58 reader reviews; publisher Wanadoo, developer Spellbound, genres Action and Aventure, single player. The editorial overall score is not rendered in the retrieved HTML; Wikipedia's table gives Jeuxvideo.com 12/20. Commercial review, so paraphrased.

- Opening: expects a Commandos-like or rather Desperados-like from Spellbound; year 1190, Richard away on crusade, Prince John's tyranny, Robin returns to find his father dead and his lands lost; praises the opening cinematic; the first mission is the family manor full of guards, used to teach the basic commands.
- Stealth balance: the reviewer, conditioned by Commandos, expected guards to notice or shout, but finds medieval guards short-sighted, deaf and easy to kill; most mistakes are forgiven; some levels can be finished by brute force, missing the point of the game.
- Possibilities: sneaking (little needed), climbing, roof jumping, shooting arrows at enemies or at targets that trigger forest traps. Verdict on design: the game "wants to do too much"; many abilities are uninteresting to use because expedient means suffice.
- Combat: draw a sword or staff and trace large crosses with the mouse; big yellow scribbles suffice for the reluctant. Real-time fights are pleasant but at odds with a concept that asks for as little fighting as possible; spared lives are counted at level end, yet map layout, guard count and placement force confrontation; manageable with one character, chaotic with several; teammates' abilities become optional except for specific obstacles.
- Presentation: 2D with three zoom levels, close-up shows pixels; attractive scenery but readability suffers, interactive objects hard to spot because of the view and the density of detail.
- Conclusion: good ideas undermined by levels that push force over puzzle; skirmishes go in your favour even five to one; the title sits awkwardly between action and tactics. Category verdicts repeat this: playability "a bit bastard", correct lifespan shortened by brute force, voices well done but quickly annoying, scenario without surprises.
